:step/content.:tutorial/content:
For a curve defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=x(t), \quad y=y(t), \qquad t\in [a,b],
$$

the arc length of the curve between $t=a$ and $t=b$ is given by

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t.
$$

Now, if we express our curve as a vector-valued function $\mathbf r(t)$ as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t)\right\rangle, \qquad t\in [a,b],
$$

we can express the arc length of the curve in a more compact form as follows:

$$
L= \int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t
$$

It's easy to see that this is equivalent to the original arc length formula. First, note that

$$
\mathbf r'(t) = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}, \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right\rangle.
$$

Calculating the magnitude of this vector, we get

$$
\|\mathbf r'(t)\| =  \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2},
$$

and thus the integral of $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ with respect to $t$ over $[a,b]$ gives the arc length of the curve.

Finally, note that we can use this arc length formula to find a curve's length in two and three dimensions.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Write down the integral that gives the arc length of the curve  $\mathbf f (t) = \langle 3 \sin t, \: 2\sin 2t \rangle$
from $t =\dfrac {3\pi} 2$  to $t = 2\pi.$

![](images/57/574a16e843a9c81e5fc9ddbbe2c0dc2c308ffcac4991bcbf48c7f45b4871c93b.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find $\mathbf f'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf f'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf g (t) = \langle 3 - 2 \sin 2t, \: 1 - 2\cos 2t \rangle$ from $t=\dfrac \pi 3$ to $\pi.$

![](images/29/29c97e5963d451cc389944ef113764b2d15998448e773a02bb98c062207c2860.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find $\mathbf g'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf g'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡2t+16{sin}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =4(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Computing the Arc Length of a Planar Curve

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given a curve $C$ parametrized by a function $\mathbf{r}(t)$, we can approximate the arc length by breaking up the curve into many small line segments and adding up their lengths.

To do this, we first choose a finite number of points $P_0,$ $P_1,$ $\cdots,$ $P_n$ along $C$ and form the polygonal path

$$
\overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/2d/2d320e6a0f63a823e049203203cbc13c210e80bc98aab5a53bcb4e5299240920.png)

Then, we can approximate the arc length as the sum of the lengths of the line segments:

$$
L \approx \, \big\| \overline{P_0P_1} \big\| + \big\| \overline{P_1P_2} \big\| + \ldots + \big\| \overline{P_{n-1}P_n} \big\|.
$$

If $P_k$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t_k),$ then by the mean value theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖\overset{―}{{P}_{k-1}{P}_{k}}‖ & =‖{r}^{'}({c}_{k})‖({t}_{k}-{t}_{k-1}) \\  & =‖{r}^{'}({c}_{k})‖Δ{t}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

for some intermediate point $c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],$ where $\Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & \approx \,‖\overset{―}{{P}_{0}{P}_{1}}‖+‖\overset{―}{{P}_{1}{P}_{2}}‖+…+‖\overset{―}{{P}_{n-1}{P}_{n}}‖ \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{n}‖{r}^{'}({c}_{k})‖Δ{t}_{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Riemann sum, and the closer the points $P_k$ are to each other, the better our approximation will be. So, in the limit as $n\to\infty$ (or $\Delta t_k \to 0),$ we have

$$
L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}  \| \mathbf r'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k=\int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/85/8573aedcd26cba038b2db072560cd3d6ba7676542888a2d9b8a356713eaf6724.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \langle \sin t ,\: \cos t, \: t \rangle$
from  $t =0$ to $t = 2\pi.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\text{ }\sqrt{2}\,t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Computing the Arc Length of a Three-Dimensional Spatial Curve

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve $C$ given by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad    t \in [0,1].
$$

 

The length of this curve is given by

$$
L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

To compute $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|,$ we take the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ and compute its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2},\,t⟩, \\ ‖{r}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{({t}^{2})^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the curve $C$ is given by the integral

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}|t|\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this integral using substitution. Let $u = t^2+1,$ then $\textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.$ Therefore, our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
